Annual Crop Land: Annual Crop Land has rectangular or square field parcels with sharp, straight boundaries that contrast with the irregular, organic shapes of Forest and Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Annual Crop Land shows a high-density mosaic of adjacent plots differing in color or texture, unlike the uniform canopy tone of Forest or the homogeneous green expanse of Pasture Land.

Annual Crop Land contains regularly spaced parallel irrigation ditches aligned precisely with field edges, whereas Permanent Crop Land lacks such dense, geometrically constrained linear drainage networks.

Annual Crop Land displays fine-grained vegetation texture with visible rows or bands of uniform height and spacing, unlike the coarser, clumped texture of Pasture Land or the vertical structure of Forest.
Annual Crop Land exhibits field parcel sizes typically between 0.5 and 5 hectares, smaller on average than the expansive, uninterrupted pastures of Pasture Land.
Annual Crop Land features access tracks forming a grid-like network intersecting at near-right angles, contrasting with the sparse, winding farm lanes typical of Permanent Crop Land.

Annual Crop Land shows strong chromatic variation across neighboring fields—such as brown soil next to green sprouts or yellow stubble—unlike the monotonous green of mature Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Annual Crop Land contains linear features (roads, furrows, ditches) oriented consistently in two dominant perpendicular directions, unlike the radial or meandering patterns seen in Forest edges.
Annual Crop Land has minimal tree cover within field interiors, distinguishing it clearly from Permanent Crop Land where trees are evenly spaced and persistent across seasons.
Annual Crop Land displays bare soil patches during planting or harvest periods, absent in the continuously vegetated surfaces of Pasture Land and Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Annual Crop Land shows field boundaries defined by narrow, dark-toned furrows or raised berms, not by hedgerows or woody vegetation lines common in Permanent Crop Land.
Annual Crop Land lacks permanent perennial vegetation structures like vine trellises or orchard grids visible at sub-meter resolution, unlike Permanent Crop Land.
Annual Crop Land contains short, low-contrast vegetation height variation across fields, unlike the pronounced vertical heterogeneity and shadow-casting crowns of Forest.
Annual Crop Land features highly reflective, smooth-surfaced soil or stubble in recently tilled fields, contrasting with the diffuse, matte reflectance of dense herbaceous canopies.
Annual Crop Land has field edges aligned to cardinal directions more frequently than Pasture Land, reflecting mechanized plowing and planting conventions.
Annual Crop Land shows abrupt transitions in surface reflectance between adjacent fields, whereas Herbaceous Vegetation Land exhibits gradual tonal blending across natural ecotones.
Annual Crop Land contains no standing water bodies larger than narrow irrigation channels, distinguishing it from flooded rice paddies misclassified as Annual Crop Land only when water is absent.
Annual Crop Land displays seasonal absence of vegetation cover over large contiguous areas, unlike the year-round ground cover of Pasture Land.
Annual Crop Land has field parcel perimeters that are predominantly convex polygons with fewer than eight vertices, unlike the sinuous, concave-rich boundaries of natural forest fragments.
Annual Crop Land shows uniformly low vegetation density during early growth stages, with visible soil between rows, unlike the interstitial bare soil scarcity in dense, matted Pasture Land.
Forest: Forest is a land cover dominated by contiguous patches of dense tree canopy with irregular, organic shapes that follow natural topography rather than rectangular field boundaries.
Forest exhibits a high-density vegetation texture appearing as fine-grained, mottled green to dark green at medium resolution, lacking the uniform smoothness of water or bare soil.
Forest shows minimal to no visible paved roads, with any linear features being narrow, winding, and discontinuous rather than straight, grid-aligned, or regularly spaced.
Forest has very low building density, with structures either absent or extremely sparse and irregularly scattered, unlike the clustered or linear arrangements seen in built-up areas or farmsteads.
Forest displays soft, diffuse edges where vegetation meets other land covers, contrasting sharply with the sharp, angular boundaries typical of Annual Crop Land or Permanent Crop Land.
Forest contains no visible geometric field patterns such as parallel rows, uniform rectangles, or repetitive tiling that characterize Herbaceous Vegetation Land or Pasture Land.
Forest lacks the regularly spaced, evenly sized circular or rectangular clearings often associated with orchards in Permanent Crop Land.
Forest shows no evidence of recent soil disturbance like plowed furrows, harrowed lines, or freshly exposed earth that appear seasonally in Annual Crop Land.
Forest has no visible irrigation infrastructure such as center-pivot circles, parallel ditches, or grid-like canal networks common in irrigated crop lands.
Forest exhibits terrain-following spatial continuity—vegetation wraps around hills and valleys without abrupt breaks—unlike the flat, parcel-level uniformity of many crop fields.
Forest contains no visible pasture fencing patterns such as parallel, evenly spaced linear segments dividing uniform grassy areas.
Forest shows no patchwork mosaic of alternating bare soil and low-vegetation zones characteristic of rotational cropping systems in Annual Crop Land.
Forest lacks the open, low-canopy structure and uniform light-green hue of Herbaceous Vegetation Land, instead presenting darker, vertically layered green tones.
Forest contains no linear road grids or orthogonal street networks that define urban or peri-urban agricultural settlements adjacent to Pasture Land.
Forest has no visible water bodies larger than small, naturally formed streams or ponds—unlike the engineered reservoirs or retention basins sometimes embedded in crop landscapes.
Forest displays multi-scale texture: coarse canopy gaps intermixed with fine leaf-level variation, unlike the homogeneous mid-green texture of dense grassland in Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Forest shows no evidence of livestock congregation patterns such as clustered dung stains, trampled paths, or concentrated shade structures found in intensively managed Pasture Land.
Forest contains no regularly spaced, aligned tree rows or widely spaced individual trees with uniform spacing indicative of orchards in Permanent Crop Land.
Forest has no visible harvested stubble, residue piles, or recently cut swaths that appear after mowing or grazing in Pasture Land or Herbaceous Vegetation Land.

Forest exhibits vertical structural complexity visible as variable brightness and shadow contrast across the canopy surface, unlike the flatter, more uniformly lit appearance of low-stature herbaceous or cropped vegetation.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land: Herbaceous Vegetation Land is a broad, irregularly shaped patch of land cover without the straight edges or right angles typical of cultivated Annual Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows continuous, soft-textured vegetation surfaces without the dense, vertically structured canopy and shadow contrast characteristic of Forest.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land displays green to yellow-brown tones with gradual color transitions, unlike the sharper seasonal color shifts and uniform row patterns seen in Annual Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land lacks the regularly spaced, parallel linear features of irrigation ditches or crop rows that define Annual Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land contains no visible orchard or vineyard grid patterns, distinguishing it from Permanent Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land exhibits low structural density with few or no buildings, contrasting sharply with the clustered built structures often found in Pasture Land near farmsteads.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has no visible fencing lines or grazing track networks that commonly segment Pasture Land into smaller enclosures.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows no evidence of recent soil disturbance or bare earth strips between planted rows, unlike actively tilled Annual Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land features naturalistic, meandering boundaries rather than the geometric parcel divisions typical of Permanent Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land lacks the high-contrast, dark-green closed-canopy texture and dendritic shadow patterns of mature Forest.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land contains no linear road networks dividing land into rectangular blocks, a hallmark of engineered agricultural layouts in Annual Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows uniform low-height vegetation coverage without the scattered tall trees or groves interspersed across Pasture Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has no visible trellis systems, support posts, or aligned planting beds that characterize Permanent Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land displays diffuse, organic edge transitions with adjacent land covers, unlike the abrupt, straight-line boundaries common in cultivated fields.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land contains no water bodies large enough to dominate the scene, distinguishing it from wetland-influenced Pasture Land or flooded rice paddies.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows no evidence of livestock congregation areas such as shaded pens or watering trough clusters found in intensively managed Pasture Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land lacks the fine-scale rectilinear texture of greenhouse complexes or plastic mulch rows seen in some Permanent Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land exhibits homogeneous surface reflectance without the periodic brightness variations caused by alternating crop rows in Annual Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has no visible access roads leading to centralized barns or silos, a pattern frequently observed in Pasture Land infrastructure.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows no canopy gaps aligned along service roads or harvesting paths, a structural signature of managed Forest harvest zones.
Highway or Road: Highway or Road is a long, narrow, straight or gently curved linear feature with sharp, well-defined edges.
Highway or Road appears as a continuous gray, white, or asphalt-dark band contrasting sharply with adjacent green vegetation or brown bare soil.
Highway or Road exhibits parallel edge pairs extending over long distances without tapering or branching irregularly.
Highway or Road forms angular intersections—typically at 90 or 120 degrees—unlike the meandering, organic bends of rivers.
Highway or Road occupies a consistent width along its length, unlike residential buildings which cluster in irregularly sized blocks.
Highway or Road lacks the fine-textured, high-contrast rooftop patterns seen in industrial buildings.
Highway or Road shows no internal texture variation across its surface, whereas herbaceous vegetation land displays mottled, granular, or streaky brightness patterns.
Highway or Road runs uninterrupted through built-up areas without the patchy gaps and variable orientation typical of residential building clusters.
Highway or Road has uniform reflectance across its entire length, unlike rivers which show specular highlights or dark, sinuous flow paths.
Highway or Road forms rigid corridor structures that segment and connect urban blocks, unlike the dense, contiguous footprints of industrial buildings.
Highway or Road displays no evidence of shadow-casting vertical structures along its length, distinguishing it from rows of residential buildings.
Highway or Road appears as a single dominant linear element within a scene, whereas herbaceous vegetation land covers broad, non-linear expanses.
Highway or Road maintains geometric continuity across changes in surrounding land cover, unlike rivers that terminate or widen at confluences.
Highway or Road lacks the dendritic or branching network structure characteristic of river systems.
Highway or Road shows no seasonal color shifts or growth-related texture changes visible in herbaceous vegetation land.
Highway or Road is flanked by abrupt transitions to adjacent land cover, not the gradual, diffuse ecotones seen at riverbanks.
Highway or Road contains no surface water pixels or reflective sheen, differentiating it clearly from rivers.
Highway or Road does not contain enclosed interior courtyards or irregular voids like those common in residential building complexes.
Highway or Road aligns precisely with orthogonal street grids, unlike the haphazard or radial layouts sometimes found around industrial buildings.
Highway or Road has minimal or no vegetation growing directly on its surface, in contrast to herbaceous vegetation land where plant coverage is complete and continuous.
Industrial Buildings: Industrial Buildings have large, contiguous patches of rectilinear buildings with sharp, angular outlines and minimal curvature.
Industrial Buildings exhibit building footprints that are significantly larger on average than those in Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings show highly regular, grid-like or parallel arrangements of structures unlike the irregular clustering in Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings display extensive impervious cover dominated by uniform gray, white, or charcoal tones without the warm beige or reddish roof hues common in Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings contain sparse, isolated patches of vegetation with low density and high fragmentation compared to the denser, more continuous greenery in Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings feature wide, straight access roads with high pavement coverage and minimal sidewalks or landscaping, unlike the narrower, curving streets in Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings occupy land parcels with higher average building density per hectare than Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings lack the fine-scale street network branching and cul-de-sacs typical of Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings show minimal presence of small-scale water features like ponds or fountains that occasionally appear in Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings have roof surfaces that are predominantly flat and unbroken by dormers, chimneys, or pitched sections common in Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings contain long, uninterrupted linear structures such as warehouse sheds exceeding 100 meters in length, unlike the shorter, segmented buildings in Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings exhibit minimal variation in building height across a site, whereas Residential Buildings often show mixed heights including multi-story apartments and single-story homes.
Industrial Buildings have parking lots that are vast, uniformly paved, and directly adjacent to buildings, unlike the smaller, dispersed, and often shaded driveways in Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings show no evidence of residential-scale infrastructure like fences, patios, or backyard gardens visible at satellite resolution.
Industrial Buildings lack the fine-grained texture of tree canopies over rooftops seen in many Residential Buildings.

Industrial Buildings display road networks optimized for heavy vehicle movement—featuring wide turning radii and minimal intersections—unlike the frequent, tight intersections in Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings have building orientations aligned consistently with cardinal directions or major transport corridors, contrasting with the varied orientation angles in Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings contain few or no rooftop solar panels compared to the increasing prevalence in Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings show no discernible pattern of individual lot boundaries or property lines visible as low walls or hedges, unlike Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings feature loading docks and large, unmarked exterior doorways spaced regularly along building perimeters, absent in Residential Buildings.
Pasture Land: Pasture Land is a large, contiguous land parcel with smooth, gently curved or straight field boundaries that are more regular than natural vegetation edges but less geometrically precise than annual crop fields.
Pasture Land shows dominant green to yellow-brown tones across broad areas, with color uniformity greater than Forest and less mottled than Herbaceous Vegetation Land.

Pasture Land exhibits low building density, with only occasional isolated farm structures scattered across open terrain, unlike the clustered dwellings of rural residential or the near-absence of buildings in Forest.
Pasture Land displays a patch-scale texture that is smoother and more homogeneous than the fine-grained, irregular mosaics of Annual Crop Land.

Pasture Land contains sparse, widely spaced linear features such as narrow farm tracks or unpaved service roads, contrasting with the dense, orthogonal road grids of urban classes and the absence of engineered lines in natural Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Pasture Land has field boundaries that are often aligned with topographic contours rather than strict right angles, distinguishing it from the rigidly rectangular layouts typical of Annual Crop Land.
Pasture Land shows minimal surface water presence—no visible ponds, rivers, or irrigation channels—unlike some Herbaceous Vegetation Land or flooded rice paddies in Annual Crop Land.

Pasture Land features vegetation density that is moderate and even, lacking the tall, vertically structured canopy of Forest and the short, patchy regrowth seen in recently grazed Herbaceous Vegetation Land.

Pasture Land occupies broad, gently rolling to flat expanses where slope-induced segmentation is subtle, unlike the steep, fragmented patterns of Forest or the terraced geometry of Permanent Crop Land.
Pasture Land lacks the high-contrast, repetitive geometric patterns of orchard rows or vineyard trellises found in Permanent Crop Land.
Pasture Land contains no visible seasonal planting lines or harvested stubble bands that characterize Annual Crop Land at certain growth stages.
Pasture Land shows no evidence of regularly spaced tree canopies or vertical shadows indicative of Forest, nor does it display the clumped shrub forms of some Herbaceous Vegetation Land.

Pasture Land has a spatial organization where adjacent parcels share similar tonal values and texture, reflecting consistent management, unlike the abrupt tonal shifts between different crop types in Annual Crop Land.
Pasture Land exhibits low edge density per unit area—few internal divisions within a parcel—compared to the high internal fragmentation of mixed-use agricultural mosaics or urban fringes.
Pasture Land displays muted, diffuse shadowing across the surface due to low vegetation height, in contrast to the sharp, elongated shadows cast by mature trees in Forest.
Pasture Land shows no visible irrigation infrastructure such as center-pivot circles, drip-line patterns, or canal networks that appear in intensively managed Annual or Permanent Crop Land.
Pasture Land maintains consistent vegetation cover year-round in temperate zones, avoiding the bare-soil phases common in Annual Crop Land after harvest.

Pasture Land has field shapes that follow property lines or natural barriers like ridges or streams, resulting in irregular but human-delineated polygons, unlike the geologically constrained shapes of natural Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Pasture Land contains no visible fruit-bearing structures, trellises, or pruning scars that distinguish Permanent Crop Land.
Pasture Land shows uniform spectral response across large swaths—no alternating bands of different crops or fallow fields—as seen in diversified Annual Crop Land.
Permanent Crop Land: Permanent Crop Land has large contiguous parcels with sharp, straight-edged boundaries that are more geometrically regular than the irregular, fragmented edges of Forest.
Permanent Crop Land shows rectangular or elongated plot shapes arranged in tightly spaced, parallel rows unlike the amorphous, clumpy shapes of Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Permanent Crop Land exhibits uniform vegetation texture within each parcel, lacking the patchy, variable density seen in Pasture Land.
Permanent Crop Land contains internal straight farm access tracks aligned orthogonally to plot edges, whereas Annual Crop Land often lacks such persistent internal linear infrastructure.
Permanent Crop Land displays consistent canopy height and density across parcels, contrasting with the highly variable vertical structure and gaps typical of Forest.
Permanent Crop Land features terraced plots on slopes with evenly spaced, parallel contour lines, unlike the natural, uneven ridges and gullies of unmanaged hillsides.
Permanent Crop Land has high spectral contrast between adjacent parcels due to uniform planting, while Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows gradual, low-contrast transitions between patches.

Permanent Crop Land shows dense, closed-canopy woody vegetation with fine-grained texture at medium resolution, unlike the coarse, sparse, or bare-soil texture of Annual Crop Land during fallow periods.
Permanent Crop Land contains regularly spaced, narrow linear gaps between rows that persist year-round, unlike the seasonal, wide, and irregularly distributed bare soil furrows of Annual Crop Land.
Permanent Crop Land maintains consistent greenness and canopy cover through dry seasons, whereas Pasture Land often turns brown, patchy, or unvegetated under drought stress.
Permanent Crop Land has smooth, homogeneous surface texture within plots due to uniform tree spacing, in contrast to the rough, heterogeneous texture of natural shrubland.
Permanent Crop Land displays high edge density per unit area from parcel boundaries, exceeding the low edge density of large, unbroken Forest stands.
Permanent Crop Land shows aligned, parallel linear features (e.g., trellises or drip lines) visible as subtle sub-meter patterns, absent in Pasture Land and Forest.
Permanent Crop Land contains no buildings or residential structures within cropped parcels, distinguishing it from mixed-use agricultural settlements found in some Annual Crop Land areas.
Permanent Crop Land lacks the dendritic, branching pattern of natural river networks, instead showing straight or gently curved drainage ditches aligned with plot geometry.
Permanent Crop Land has minimal or no surface water bodies within parcels, unlike flooded rice paddies or wetland-influenced Herbaceous Vegetation Land.

Permanent Crop Land exhibits strong directional alignment of all major linear features—plots, tracks, and rows—in a single dominant orientation, unlike the multi-directional field patterns sometimes seen in smallholder Annual Crop Land.
Permanent Crop Land shows uniform medium-brightness NDVI values across entire parcels, whereas Forest displays higher, more saturated NDVI with greater intra-parcel variability.
Permanent Crop Land contains no visible grazing animals or animal trails, differentiating it from actively used Pasture Land where such traces are often detectable.

Permanent Crop Land has sharply defined parcel borders with abrupt spectral transitions, unlike the diffuse, ecotonal blending between vegetation types in natural Forest–Herbaceous Vegetation Land boundaries.
Residential Buildings: Residential Buildings have small to medium rectangular building footprints arranged in repeating grid-like patterns with consistent spacing between structures.
Residential Buildings show narrow, branching street networks forming closed loops and cul-de-sacs, unlike the long straight segments and high-speed interchanges of Highway or Road.
Residential Buildings exhibit low-to-medium building density with visible gaps between structures, contrasting with the contiguous, wall-to-wall coverage typical of Industrial Buildings.
Residential Buildings feature roofs predominantly in muted grays, whites, and light tans, whereas Industrial Buildings often display large expanses of corrugated metal in silvers or rust tones.
Residential Buildings occupy parcels that are uniformly sized and aligned, unlike the irregular, organically shaped plots common in Annual Crop Land.
Residential Buildings include driveways as short linear features extending perpendicularly from streets to individual buildings, unlike the wide, uninterrupted pavement of Highway or Road.
Residential Buildings display a moderate proportion of impervious surface—less than Industrial Buildings but more than Permanent Crop Land—which appears as interconnected gray and black patches.

Residential Buildings contain scattered, small-to-medium deciduous or coniferous trees within yards, creating a dappled, medium-density vegetation texture unlike the uniform canopy of Permanent Crop Land.
Residential Buildings show sharp-edged, angular building outlines with right-angle corners, distinguishing them from the soft, curving boundaries and irregular shapes of Annual Crop Land.
Residential Buildings are organized into clusters of 5–20 structures sharing similar orientation and scale, unlike the isolated or linear arrangements of Industrial Buildings.
Residential Buildings lack large, unbroken paved areas exceeding 100 meters in length, which are characteristic of Highway or Road.
Residential Buildings have roof shapes dominated by simple gables and hipped forms, not the flat, expansive, or sawtooth profiles common in Industrial Buildings.
Residential Buildings include sidewalks as thin parallel lines adjacent to streets, absent in both Annual Crop Land and Permanent Crop Land.
Residential Buildings show parcel boundaries defined by low fences, hedges, or driveways, forming regular polygons unlike the field-scale straight edges of Annual Crop Land.
Residential Buildings contain backyard spaces with patchy grass or shrub cover, producing a mottled green texture distinct from the smooth, homogeneous green of Permanent Crop Land.
Residential Buildings feature street lighting poles spaced regularly along residential roads, a detail absent in Highway or Road where lighting is taller and less frequent per kilometer.
Residential Buildings have minimal or no large water bodies within their immediate footprint, unlike the ponds or irrigation ditches sometimes embedded in Annual Crop Land.
Residential Buildings display rooftop solar panels only sporadically and at low density, whereas Industrial Buildings may show dense, uniform arrays on large flat roofs.
Residential Buildings lack the large loading docks, rail spurs, or stacked shipping containers visible in Industrial Buildings.

Residential Buildings contain swimming pools as small blue rectangles oriented orthogonally to houses, unlike the long, narrow, linear water bodies associated with irrigation canals in Annual Crop Land.
River: River is a narrow, sinuous linear feature with gently curving bends and variable width that tapers gradually along its course.
River appears as a continuous dark blue or grayish-blue strip that maintains consistent tonal continuity over long distances without abrupt terminations.
River has sharply defined, smooth-edged boundaries that contrast strongly against adjacent vegetated or bare soil areas.
River lacks the large, enclosed, static shape typical of lakes and instead forms an open-ended, branching or meandering network.
River shows no evidence of parallel straight edges or uniform width like highways, instead exhibiting irregular lateral variation in channel width.
River displays fine-textured or glassy surface appearance distinct from the coarse, mottled texture of forest canopies.
River occupies a topographically constrained corridor, often following valleys or depressions, unlike roads which frequently cut across slopes or follow grid patterns.
River is darker in tone than most roads, which commonly appear light gray, white, or tan due to paved surfaces.
River lacks the geometric regularity of agricultural fields, showing no repeated rectangular or parallel patterns in its form or surroundings.
River does not contain internal linear alignments such as crop rows, fence lines, or building footprints that characterize farmland or urban areas.
River exhibits branching tributary structures that converge downstream, unlike isolated or parallel road segments.
River has no visible surface markings like lane dividers, shoulders, or intersections that distinguish highways and roads.
River appears as a single dominant linear element within its corridor, whereas forests consist of many small, densely packed, irregularly shaped canopy patches.
River reflects sky or ambient light with subtle specular highlights along its length, unlike the diffuse reflectance of vegetated land covers.
River maintains visual connectivity across varied terrain, including hills and ridges, while roads often terminate or switch direction abruptly at topographic barriers.
River shows gradual transitions in color and width corresponding to changes in flow volume, unlike the abrupt starts and stops typical of short road segments.
River lacks the high-density clustering of rectangular, angular shapes associated with built-up areas or industrial zones.
River is typically flanked by narrow, irregular riparian zones rather than the wide, uniform buffer strips sometimes seen alongside major highways.
River displays subtle variations in tone along its length due to depth changes, whereas seas and lakes show more uniform, expansive tonal fields.
River avoids sharp 90-degree turns and rigid angular geometry, distinguishing it from urban street grids and engineered canals.
Sea or Lake: Sea or Lake is a large, contiguous expanse of water with no visible field boundaries or agricultural grid patterns unlike Herbaceous Vegetation Land or Pasture Land.
Sea or Lake appears as a broad, smooth surface lacking the fine linear texture of river channels and showing no meandering or branching geometry typical of rivers.
Sea or Lake displays uniform dark blue, blue-green, or gray tones across its entire visible area without the patchy green hues or variable brightness of Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Sea or Lake has sharply defined, often irregular shorelines that separate it from adjacent land, whereas rivers show continuous linear corridors bounded by vegetation or banks.
Sea or Lake lacks the dense network of straight, parallel, or orthogonal road-like patterns seen in built-up areas and absent in River, Herbaceous Vegetation Land, and Pasture Land.
Sea or Lake exhibits specular sun-glint patches scattered across its surface, a feature not found on vegetated lands or narrow river corridors.
Sea or Lake occupies a dominant, central area in the scene with no internal segmentation into smaller units, unlike Pasture Land which often shows fenced or divided paddocks.
Sea or Lake shows no evidence of vegetation texture—no mottled green reflectance, no clumpy or striated canopy patterns—distinguishing it clearly from Herbaceous Vegetation Land and Pasture Land.
Sea or Lake has no discernible flow direction indicators such as sediment plumes, sinuous narrowing, or confluence points that characterize rivers.
Sea or Lake presents a near-textureless surface at medium resolution, contrasting with the granular or stippled appearance of herbaceous vegetation canopies.
Sea or Lake contains no linear features resembling roads, tracks, or hedgerows that commonly fragment Pasture Land or Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Sea or Lake maintains consistent tone and reflectance across wide distances without the tonal gradation or moisture-related streaking typical of river surfaces.
Sea or Lake lacks the clustered, rectangular, or irregular building footprints and associated shadow patterns found in urban or peri-urban areas but not in the confusable siblings.
Sea or Lake shows no evidence of rotational or concentric planting patterns, crop rows, or irrigation circles that may appear in adjacent agricultural lands but never on open water.
Sea or Lake has no visible shoreline vegetation fringe wider than a few pixels, unlike rivers which often display continuous riparian strips.
Sea or Lake occupies topographic lows but appears as a static, unbroken surface without the directional alignment or valley-constrained path of rivers.
Sea or Lake displays no evidence of tidal flats, exposed mudflats, or intertidal zones within its main body—features that would suggest coastal transition rather than open water.
Sea or Lake has no internal color variation indicating submerged vegetation, algal blooms, or shallow-water bottom reflectance that might mimic Pasture Land or Herbaceous Vegetation Land tones.

Sea or Lake shows no evidence of dam structures, spillways, or engineered embankments that distinguish reservoirs from natural lakes—but reservoirs still belong to this class and share its visual attributes.

Sea or Lake exhibits high reflectance uniformity across its surface, with minimal local variance compared to the higher spatial variance in brightness and color seen in Pasture Land and Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
